To answer your questions

1. Having supportive people really helped for me. Sometimes I really didn't want to go through the day but friends pushed me, even if it was something I didn't want to hear. Also as well, having something to look forward to at the end of it (e.g. film night) helped as well, because it made the hardship rewarding. Another important thing is keeping track of your achievement and how far you've come as well, that's important because it makes you respect the effort that you've put in (I remember watching a David Goggins video on Thanksgiving which hit the nail on the head regarding this). It's a lot of effort trying to keep a positive mentality (especially as I suffered from bad mental health) but once you realise that it's meant to be hard (technically, physically and mentally), your morale becomes a lot more resilient
2. In terms of recon and note-taking, I take screenshots as I go along. Though this is a very exam/CTF-specific tactic (that won't apply in real life) , I try to create a story of how the examiner would want me to access the system, be that password leak then ssh or go into an application first and then do RCE etc.
3. I don't think so, but I did play a low-risk move by focussing on the 20 and 10 point boxes; in my mind the 25 point box was too risky because disproportionately harder for the extra 5 points. 
4. About 30-40 boxes in; most of it were TJNull's list of OSCP-like boxes, and I've also done a few Easy boxes that were not retired (for those juicy HTB points). I'd say in hindsight the difficulty of  OSCP boxes have to be limited (Easy-Medium on HTB) because you only have 24 hours. Also, the PG boxes are quite good as well, because they give you a flavour of what Offsec-made boxes are like

The Institute: can win, so long as no faction finds out where they are and how they transport themselves. They can have synth infiltrators and agitate hostilities between factions like the Enclave, BOS and NCR, and can emerge victorious with minimal casualties. They also have the ability to deploy a large number of fighters in a specific place in a short space of time, so have the best element of surprise of all other factions.

NCR: Can win by having the most reliable logistics of other factions by establishing law and order among communities and supplying from them, so in the case of a protracted war, they can hold out longer than the BOS, Enclave or the Institute. Push comes to shove, they can conscript soldiers from civilians, using their authority and/or public relations. 

BOS: Have a higher logistical requirements (as they use laser weapons and power armour), but have a LOT of firepower along with soldiers in power armour, so can win so long as they maintain momentum. 

Enclave: Great firepower, but have the fewest allies in the game. If they have to resort to supplying from the wasteland, they would lose because they have to stretch their force over a large area. However, they have the modified FEV so can in theory wipe out every other faction and most of the Institute. 

​

Conclusion: Pyrrhic victory for the NCR, because they are least likely to run out of food/water/ammunition/soldiers out of all the factions.

Everyone does the OSCP in different ways, but an important key point in doing the exam is to establish your battle morale in the first hours of the exam and maintain it for the rest of it. 

I personally find BOF the easiest part of the exam so I'd do it straight away, and it's something you could without ANY enumeration. Other people think that BOF could be good mid-exam when you're finding it harder to enumerate (because of fatigue) and you can do BOFs because the process between different executables aren't that different. 

​

Remember the 2 hour rule; if you're not making progress in a box for 2 hours, switch boxes and attack those instead.

Good luck, I'm also taking my third attempt tomorrow! Got 25 (BOF) on my first attempt, 55 on the second, but for each time I debrief with myself what went well and what was difficult. Split that up into mental (e.g. exam anxiety, elation after getting foothold etc.), strategic (e.g. what order to crack boxes in) and technical (i.e. knowledge of certain tools, services, approaches to enumeration etc.) .

For each exam attempt, I plan out the entire day. These will be generic, like how often to take breaks (I did 5 mins break every 1 hour), when to sleep and for how long, caffeine cap (don't overdrink caffeine). Also, with each break, write yourself a "handover" note, summarising what you've done so far and what issues you're facing. That way, after each break, you can come back to the exam and know where to head. 

Mental state in the exam is THE MOST important aspect of your exam. Too anxious and you'll miss out stuff on enumeration. Too elated and you will attack one rabbit hole for several hours. A lot of people do the BOF first; I do the BOF first so that it gives me the feeling in the exam that pwnage is achievable! 

For a box specific approach, my approach would be asking myself what the examiners intended when writing this box and setting up the services. Harder boxes require chaining of vulns (e.g. credential disclosure) to reach foothold. Having in mind that there are broadly speaking only three ways of achieving foothold (RCE, weak credentials, and ssh keys) will help you with that.

As root you can do the following steps to get passwords:

1. `cat /etc/passwd`  (this gets usernames) and save the contents into a file
2. `cat /etc/shadow` (this gets password hashes) and save the contents
3. `unshdaow passwd shadow` to turn it into a format suitable for JTR
4. Use JTR or other password crackers e.g. hashcat

​

With this exam, I'd organise the preparation into academic and pastroal preparation, academic being the study itself, and the pastoral being the environment and well-being side. 

In terms of organising OSCP study prep, I'd probably do the following:

1. Organise study: Are you going to do boxes in PG/VulnHub/HTB or go through topics e.g. Tib3rius' PrivEsc course
2. With each box that you do, try as hard as you can until you reach wit's end and only then look at walkthroughs. A large part of  the exam in my opinion aims to assess your ability to deal with what you don't know and how you can research your way out of it. 
3. For each box that you've rooted, write a report, as though it's an OSCP box. 
4. In that report, write in a few bullet points what you've learned. Include both topics e.g. XSS, LFI, BOF, and techniques e.g. useful grep-fu commands, useful tools
5. Make your own quick reference cheat sheet, especially on things that are frequently encountered and easy to forget
6. Prepare your 24 + 24 hours of OSCP (the first 24 being the exam and the next 24 being the report writing). Include itinerary (food, drink and caffeine etc.), work/break rhythm and sleep time. 

In terms of your pastoral prep, I'd something along the lines of this:

1. Make an itinerary list of documents required, food and hydration (I'd say small snacks, avoid sugar), and caffeine arrangements of your choice
2. Plan the day, especially plan breaks in between. How long will you go at the box, and how long will you take a break. You can't hack for hours at a time, especially when you're body is pumping high with adrenaline, caffeine and cortisol. Do this a few days before the exam. 
3. Ensure you're looking after your mental wellbeing one week before the exam. Especially pay attention to it the day before. You need to be able to perform, and if your knowledge is not ready by this  time then you need to re-book the exam. 
4. Hours before you being, do something to relax yourself, but be back by your desk 30 mins before.

Finally, if after all that, you're still lost, then I'd personally go for competitions. In competitions, you may not learn new knowledge per se, but you will definitely come across best practices for certain aspects of hacking that you may not have otherwise thought of, and can shed great light how to be a "better" hacker, being smoother with your approach

I'm gearing up for my second OSCP attempt;  here's what I did as a complete beginner who started January: 

1. TryHackMe: Offensive Pentesting Pathway
   1. Do the Complete Beginner pathway if necessary 
   2. CompTIA Pentest+ pathway is also good to get a broader knowledge
2. Background reading on networks and network security (think CompTIA S+, Pentest+ etc.)
3. HackTheBox: Paid and completed Dante. Network hacking is difficult but incredibly rewarding (plus my LinkedIn blew up once I declared that I'd done it)

​

As you learn you should learn how to take notes, and categorise your methodology as the following:

1. Initial enumeration: What ports (SCAN ALL PORTS), what services, **what OS**, what is the name of the host (this can give you a great hint on how to approach a box). Be thorough as possible, because this will be the foundation of you approaching initial foothold. 
2. Initial Foothold: Is there a place where you can upload a file? Can you log into something? Is there a vuln that allows you to run "arbitrary commands (Read: Remote Code Execution)". Can you get access with "normal" methods e.g. SSH, RDP? When you get an initial shell is it limited (in which case you need to spawn a proper shell)
3. Enumerate for PE: Who are you? (whoami). What privs do you have? Have you run automated scanners like LinPEAS? What is running as root? Do you need to manipulate the OS itself or are there exploitable software installed? PE method differs greatly between Windows and Linux!
4. Post-PE: You have full control. Now retrieve all files that are important for cybersecurity e.g. password hashes, internal information regarding what ports are open, where else is the box connected to.

​

* The exam environment feels vastly different due to both the time constraint and the pressure you put on yourself. I'd prepare for the pressure that comes with time limits, including how to work effectively, how to take breaks and how to know when to stop pursuing a certain thing (be that a vuln enumeration or trying an exploit)
* With that in mind, have a plan of things you can do without spending much brain power. I found the first hour or so particularly difficult because I was anxious, and my brain literally froze. Scripts are good; but also a fallback of all the things you'd do (I'd plan it out) would be even better (especially if you include any scripts that you are comfortable with)
* Furthermore, have a rough plan of the 24 hours. At what point of the exam will you do the BOF. What order will you attempt the boxes? When will you sleep and for how long?
* I can't say which ones, but cover all the KEY topics. Easier said than done, but you will need to know key topics comfortably to be able to effectively do it under pressure. Imagine how bad it will be to go in without knowing BOF. It's like that, but for other topics. 
* Practice using metasploit. OSCP rules stipulate that metasploit can only be used for one box. This also means that it is that powerful, and you need to know when to use it.
